records.title: Epidemiology, Fracture Patterns, and Risk Factors Among Motorcycle Crash Victims Treated at Orthopedic Institute, Tanzania.
records.abstract: Motorcycle crashes are a leading cause of injury and death in low- and middle-income countries, yet detailed data on fracture patterns and severity determinants remain limited in East Africa. This study aimed to characterize the epidemiology, fracture patterns, and associated risk factors among motorcycle crash victims treated at Muhimbili Orthopaedic Institute (MOI). A hospital-based cross-sectional study included 273 motorcyclists with confirmed fractures treated at MOI between January and December 2024. Data on demographics, crash characteristics, injury patterns, and treatment were extracted from medical records using a structured form. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were used to identify predictors of open fractures. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Participants were predominantly male (94.5%) and aged 18-40 years (78.0%). Most were self-employed commercial riders (64.8%) paying out-of-pocket for care (86.8%). High-risk behaviors were common: 45.1% were not wearing helmets, 36.6% had consumed alcohol before riding, and 45.4% of crashes occurred at speeds >80 km/h. Lower limb fractures predominated (62.9%), with tibia/fibula fractures accounting for 39.6% and femur fractures 23.4%. Open fractures represented 43.2% of cases. Crashes clustered during night/early morning and morning peak hours (44.1% each), whereas motorcycle-motorcycle collisions were the commonest crash mechanism (50.9%). On chi-square analysis, speed at impact (p = 0.034) and injury type (p < 0.001) were significantly associated with fracture severity, whereas helmet nonuse showed a nonsignificant trend (p = 0.090). In multivariable logistic regression, lower limb injury was the only independent predictor of open fractures (AOR = 3.42, 95% CI: 1.92-6.09, p < 0.001). Higher riding speeds showed a trend toward increased odds of open fractures but did not reach statistical significance after adjustment (p = 0.059 for the overall speed category variable). Motorcycle crashes in this setting predominantly affect young male riders and frequently result in severe lower limb injuries, with a substantial burden of open fractures requiring resource-intensive surgical care. Lower limb injury was the only independent predictor of open fractures. Speeding, helmet nonuse, and alcohol consumption were highly prevalent modifiable exposures but were not independently associated with open fracture status after adjustment. Drawing on external evidence, strengthening enforcement of speed limits and helmet legislation, implementing workplace-based safety programs for commercial riders, enhancing trauma and orthopedic surgical capacity, and expanding financial protection mechanisms for injured riders are recommended.

records.title: Estrogen Receptor Expression Changes After Puberty in the Porcine Anterior Cruciate Ligament.
records.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries disproportionately affect female adolescent athletes, with hormonal influences implicated in this sex disparity. However, the relationship between pubertal hormonal changes and ACL gene and protein expression remains poorly understood. This study characterized hormone receptor expression and transcriptional profiles in the anteromedial (AM) and posterolateral (PL) bundles of female porcine ACLs before and after puberty. ACL bundles were collected from pre-pubescent (8 weeks) and post-pubescent (> 8 months) female Yorkshire cross-breed pigs (n = 6/group) and analyzed using gene expression profiling, western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Pre-pubescent ACLs exhibited greater expression of primary matrix genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, ELN, TNMD), suggesting active matrix synthesis, while post-pubescent ACLs showed elevated secondary matrix genes (COL3A1, LUM, COMP), indicating a homeostatic state. Notably, estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) gene and protein expression were significantly greater in post-pubescent ACLs, particularly in AM bundles, whereas G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30) expression was elevated pre-puberty. Both receptors were distributed homogeneously throughout the tissue. Histologically, post-pubescent ACLs demonstrated decreased cellularity and thicker fascicles compared to pre-pubescent tissues. These findings indicate that ACL sensitivity to estrogen varies across development, with increased ERα expression post-puberty potentially rendering the ligament more responsive to circulating estrogen. This work provides foundational evidence for age-dependent hormonal responsiveness in the ACL and motivates further investigation into how sex hormones influence ACL injury risk in adolescent females.

records.title: Evaluating effects of a new hip-knee-ankle-foot orthosis on gait parameters in healthy individuals.
records.abstract: Hip-knee-ankle-foot orthoses (HKAFOs) are commonly used to assist gait; however, conventional designs are associated with high energy expenditure and poor mediolateral balance. This pilot study examined whether permitting additional motion in selected hip and ankle planes altered joint kinematics and dynamic-balance parameters in healthy participants. A randomized cross-over trial was conducted with 20 healthy participants aged 18-25. Gait performance was evaluated under five conditions: conventional HKAFO (locked/unlocked knee), Multiflex HKAFO (locked/unlocked knee), and no orthosis. Kinematic and balance data were collected. Key variables analyzed included center of pressure (CoP) velocity, mediolateral sway, and joint range of motion (ROM). Compared with the conventional HKAFO configurations, the Multiflex HKAFO permitted greater abduction/adduction and ankle inversion/eversion ROM. With the Multiflex HKAFO and an unlocked knee joint, CoP velocity and mediolateral excursion were not significantly different from walking without an orthosis. However, knee flexion/extension and ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion remained restricted relative to walking without an orthosis. In healthy participants, the Multiflex HKAFO permitted greater motion in selected hip and ankle planes than the conventional design while producing lower center-of-pressure velocity and mediolateral excursion in some configurations.

records.title: Federated learning for privacy-preserving collaborative health risk classification using wearable sensor data: validation study with elite football training load monitoring.
records.abstract: Wearable sensor technologies are now widely adopted in professional sports for high-frequency health and performance monitoring during training and, in some cases, recovery periods, generating multimodal physiological and self-reported wellness data. These data carry high privacy sensitivity as protected personal health information, and in competitive sports they additionally hold tactical intelligence value. Consequently, multiorganization data sharing remains institutionally infeasible, creating data silos that constrain the scalability of data-driven health risk classification models. Federated learning (FL) has shown promise in health care for collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, but systematic empirical validation on athlete-level wearable health data with quantified, genuinely non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) characteristics-spanning label, quantity, and covariate shift-remains absent. The present study therefore aimed to determine whether FL can achieve training load risk classification performance equivalent to centralized training while keeping raw athlete health data on-device, and to systematically investigate the key factors affecting FL efficacy in heterogeneous wearable health data scenarios. The publicly available SoccerMon dataset was used, comprising daily monitoring records from 50 elite female football players (all released players retained; filtering applied at the record level only) across 2 independent teams over the 2020 and 2021 seasons (36,550 raw records). A 21-dimensional multimodal feature matrix was constructed from 7 training load metrics derived from session rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) and its exponentially weighted moving averages (including the acute: chronic workload ratio [ACWR]), 7 subjective wellness indicators, and 7 binary missingness indicators. Using 28-day sliding windows, the future 7-day mean ACWR was classified into 3 risk levels (19,421 supervised samples). The federated clients exhibited three concurrent non-IID characteristics: label-distribution skew (SD of the high-risk class proportion across athlete clients 9.4% in TeamA and 21.7% in TeamB), quantity skew (mean 267-313 training windows per client), and between-team covariate shift that was statistically significant on all key training-load indicators but small in magnitude (Mann-Whitney r = .034-0.104), indicating that client-level rather than team-level heterogeneity dominates. Two-layer stacked long short-term memory (LSTM) networks served as client models within FedAvg and FedProx frameworks, compared against a centralized LSTM and 5 traditional machine learning baselines across single-team (K = 27), cross-team (K = 49), and team-level (K = 2) federated scenarios. All core experiments were repeated 30 times with Bonferroni-corrected paired t tests and Cohen d effect sizes. Team-level FedAvg retained 94.1% of centralized κ (0.401, SD 0.023 vs. 0.426, SD 0.018); cross-team athlete-level FedAvg retained 92.0% (κ = 0.392, SD 0.019); and single-team FedAvg retained 90.0% (κ = 0.366, SD 0.021). Two one-sided tests (TOST) established equivalence within a ± 0.05 κ practical bound between FL and centralized training in the cross-team and team-level scenarios (both TOST P ≤ .001), and between FedAvg and FedProx in all three scenarios (all TOST P < .001). High-risk recall remained within a narrow band across scenarios (FedAvg 0.767-0.828 vs. centralized LSTM 0.796-0.806). A naive persistence baseline reached κ of only 0.253-0.262, exceeded by FedAvg by 44.6%-53.1%, indicating that the model captures substantial structure beyond trivial autoregression. FedAvg and FedProx performed equivalently, with FedAvg approximately twice as computationally efficient. Load-only training features (7 dimensions) matched the full 21-dimensional set, and sRPE-derived internal load features contributed the majority of predictive importance. FL enables training load risk classification statistically equivalent to centralized training within a ± 0.05 κ practical bound, without sharing raw wearable health data, providing a viable privacy-preserving pathway for cross-organization sports analytics and health monitoring collaboration. These findings extend FL validation from clinical health care to athlete-level wearable health data with genuine non-IID characteristics, and remain robust under strictly causal data preprocessing.

records.title: Feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability in people with chronic ankle instability during single-leg landing.
records.abstract: Individuals with chronic ankle instability(CAI) show deficits in neuromuscular control and postural stability. While feedback mechanisms are well-studied, feedforward mechanisms during dynamic tasks remains underexplored. This study compared feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability among CAI, coper and healthy groups. Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX1s&TOTEX3s), mediolateral sway distance(DML), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p < 0.001) and PL(260 ± 87 ms vs. 102 ± 62 ms, p < 0.001) pre-activations, alongside higher TA activity(76 ± 27% vs. 35 ± 19%, p < 0.001) but lower PL activity(38 ± 14% vs. 77 ± 23%, p < 0.001). Higher RMS_ML_0.4(6.7 ± 1.3%BW vs. 5.6 ± 1.0%BW, p = 0.037), DML(55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p < 0.001) and peak vGRF(334 ± 44%BW vs. 286 ± 59%BW, p = 0.041)were observed as well. Coper showed earlier GL pre-activation(169 ± 57 ms vs. 108 ± 67 ms, p = 0.021), increased activity(155 ± 40% vs. 97 ± 29%, p < 0.001) and decreased DML(42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

records.title: FIM Motorcycling sport-specific extension of the IOC consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020.
records.abstract: In 2020, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) released a consensus statement recommending standardised methods for recording and reporting illness and injury in sport. A key component of this statement was the recognition that sport-specific extensions should be developed to provide more detailed recommendations tailored to individual sports and/or settings. In response, the Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme (FIM) Medical Commission convened a 15-member panel-comprising clinicians across multiple specialities, a sports scientist and two FIM delegates-to develop a consensus statement specific to motorcycling sport injury and illness surveillance. The panel reviewed existing consensus literature relevant to sport injury/illness surveillance and conducted two rounds of voting based on the IOC framework using a Delphi methodology. They then voted on key sport-specific recommendations to form the motorcycling sport-specific extension. The final manuscript was approved unanimously by all panel members after two rounds of revision. Relative to the parent IOC statement, this extension: (1) reframes injury categorisation and contact mechanisms around the combined rider-and-machine nature of motorcycling incidents; (2) replaces symptom-based and pathology-based severity scoring with a time-loss model adapted to the sport's irregular competition calendar, including explicit handling of estimated severity and right-censored cases; (3) restricts exposure measurement to motorcycle-mounted transponder data rather than wearable devices, for safety and regulatory reasons and (4) introduces a discipline-specific appendix covering fall/injury mechanisms, demographic and equipment-damage variables and primary/secondary exposure and severity measures across circuit racing, motocross/supercross/supermoto, trial, enduro, cross-country and track racing. The motorcycling sport-specific extension of the IOC consensus statement aims to provide researchers and governing bodies with a standardised methodology to undertake injury and illness surveillance in motorcycling sport.

records.title: Gait speed and multi-segment foot joint kinematics throughout the entire stance phase using statistical parametric mapping.
records.abstract: The foot is a multi-segment structure whose segments function together. Due to its ongoing connection with the support surface, the foot must be capable of managing loads that vary with gait speed. Previous studies have provided considerable insight into the relationship between foot joint kinematics and gait speed. However, their primary reliance on discrete measures, such as peak joint angles, has limited understanding of how these relationships evolve throughout the stance phase. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gait speed on full time-series trajectories of multiplanar foot joint kinematics using statistical parametric mapping. According to our findings, faster walking primarily increased ankle eversion and midfoot dorsiflexion during weight acceptance (∼17-29% of the stance phase). In contrast, during propulsion, faster walking increased ankle plantar flexion (∼80-100% of the stance phase) and inversion (∼82-90%), as well as midfoot plantar flexion (∼82-100%) and adduction (∼90-98%), together with greater dorsiflexion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after heel-off (∼43-98% of the stance phase). These multiplanar joint kinematic alterations across the ankle-foot joints throughout the stance phase reflect greater foot-arch collapse in early stance and foot-arch recoil in late stance, which may facilitate appropriate energy absorption and generation in response to increasing gait speed. Importantly, these adaptive foot motions were not captured by previous discrete analyses, which may obscure phase-dependent changes during gait. The present continuous time-series approach revealed detailed temporal adaptations in foot kinematics across the stance phase, providing a more comprehensive characterization of gait mechanics.

records.title: Global research on cricket injuries (1982-2025): A bibliometric analysis.
records.abstract: Cricket is one of the most widely played sports worldwide and carries a significant burden of musculoskeletal injuries, particularly among fast bowlers. Over the past four decades, research in cricket injury epidemiology, biomechanics, workload monitoring, and surveillance has expanded substantially. To conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of global cricket injury research, identifying growth trends, influential publications, leading contributors, collaboration networks, and major thematic domains. Publications from 1982 to 2025 were systematically analyzed using bibliometric indicators including annual growth, authorship productivity, institutional and country contributions, citation impact, total link strength (TLS), and co-authorship networks. The top 100 cited papers and the top 10 highly cited papers (HCPs) were examined in detail to identify landmark contributions and research priorities. A sharp rise in publications occurred after 2003, with nearly 90% of output produced in the last two decades. Australia, the United Kingdom, and South Africa led in productivity, citation impact, and collaborative link strength. The top 10 HCPs accounted for 10% of papers but 37.25% of total citations, underscoring concentrated scholarly influence. Fast bowlers consistently demonstrated the highest injury incidence, particularly lumbar spine and lower limb injuries. Workload spikes were strongly associated with increased injury risk, establishing load monitoring as a central preventive strategy. Biomechanical factors such as mixed bowling action, trunk rotation, and front-knee mechanics were linked to lumbar stress injuries. Standardized injury definitions and international consensus surveillance frameworks significantly improved research quality and comparability. Cricket injury research has evolved into a mature, collaborative, and high-impact domain centered on fast bowling biomechanics, workload regulation, and surveillance standardization. Expanded global participation and integration of advanced analytics are essential for future injury prevention strategies.

records.title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
records.abstract: As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

records.title: Hydrogel-based biosensors for sweat analysis in sports medicine: recent advances and future prospects.
records.abstract: Sweat is a physiological fluid that can be collected non-invasively and is continuously secreted by the human body. It contains a wide variety of biomarkers, including electrolytes, metabolites, hormones, and proteins, which may provide complementary information about physical activity and selected aspects of physiological status. In recent years, wearable biosensors based on hydrogels have drawn increasing interest in exercise monitoring and sports medicine because of the material's flexibility, hydrophilicity, and biocompatibility. This review summarizes recent advances in hydrogel-based sweat detection, highlighting sensing mechanisms and representative applications for four major biomarker categories: electrolytes, metabolites, hormones, and proteins. It also discusses potential applications in hydration assessment, fatigue-related monitoring, sports-injury risk assessment, and rehabilitation management. The discussion addresses current challenges, including material durability, signal stability, physiological interpretation, clinical translation, and large-scale manufacturing. Looking ahead, future progress will likely focus on multifunctional hydrogels, integration with artificial intelligence and data-driven methods, personalized monitoring, and standardized testing and validation protocols. Overall, hydrogel-based sweat biosensing offers a promising complementary approach for non-invasive physiological monitoring, although broader sports-medicine use will require rigorous validation under real-world exercise conditions.

records.title: Immediate Effects of Kinesiotaping on Lower Limb Biomechanics and Interlimb Symmetry in Return-to-Sport Athletes After ACL Reconstruction.
records.abstract: Residual biomechanical deficits may persist during landing after ACL reconstruction despite meeting return-to-sport criteria, and the immediate effects of kinesiotaping (KT) remain unclear. This study investigated bilateral lower limb biomechanics and the immediate effects of KT in 18 return-to-sport athletes after ACL reconstruction. Three-dimensional motion capture and dual force plates were used during the landing absorption phase. Statistical parametric mapping and 2-way repeated-measures analysis of variance were applied for analysis, and the limb symmetry index was calculated to assess interlimb symmetry. The uninvolved limb demonstrated greater vertical ground reaction force, loading rate, knee and ankle joint work (P < .05), hip external rotation moment (P = .025), and knee flexion moment (P < .001) than the involved limb. KT reduced knee varus and external rotation angles and internal knee valgus moment in the involved limb (P < .05) and increased bilateral hip work contribution (P = .026). However, KT did not significantly improve interlimb symmetry (P > .05). ACL reconstruction athletes meeting return-to-sport criteria continue to exhibit bilateral biomechanical asymmetries during landing. KT improved frontal- and transverse-plane knee control and promoted a more proximal energy absorption strategy, but restoring interlimb symmetry requires comprehensive neuromuscular rehabilitation.

records.title: Impacts of emotional priming during multiple object tracking tasks on drop landing strategy in individuals with functional ankle instability: an exploratory study.
records.abstract: Attentional resources play a critical role in voluntary movement execution under dual-task (DT) conditions, such as Multiple Object Tracking (MOT). Efficient resource allocation requires cognitive adjustments, which may divert attention from motor control and exacerbate movement deficits. Functional Ankle Instability (FAI) is characterized by impaired proprioception, neuromuscular dysfunction and compromised motor strategy, often resulting in inefficient landing strategies. While emotional priming has been shown to influence cognitive and motor performance, its specific impact on drop landing strategies in FAI individuals during cognitively demanding tasks remains unclear. This study aims to examine how different emotional priming conditions influence the biomechanical characteristics of drop landing strategies in individuals with FAI while performing an MOT task. Fourteen individuals with FAI and fourteen matched healthy controls participated in a drop landing experiment under dual-task (MOT) and single-task conditions. Three emotional states-Neutral Emotion (NEm), Negative Emotion (NEg), and Positive Emotion (PE)-were induced through priming. Kinematic and kinetic data were collected using a Vicon motion capture system and a Kistler force plate. A 2 × 2 × 3 mixed-design ANOVA was conducted to assess the effects of group, task conditions, and emotional state. Significant interaction effects between task condition and group were observed, especially in hip flexion at Initial Contact (IC) and knee stiffness. Under DT conditions, individuals with FAI demonstrated reduced hip flexion (p = 0.001) and increased knee stiffness (p = 0.004), indicating a rigid landing pattern. Emotional priming interacted with task condition to modulate joint kinematics and kinetics. Specifically, under DT conditions, PE enhanced ankle plantarflexion (p = 0.002) and reduced knee flexion at IC (p = 0.018), while NEm reduced hip flexion at peak Vertical Ground Reaction Force (VGRF) (p = 0.016) and increased hip stiffness (p = 0.044). In particular, following a significant three-way interaction, simple-simple effect analyses revealed that for individuals with FAI under dual-task landing, peak VGRF in the NEm condition was significantly higher than in the PE condition (p = 0.038). Under the same dual-task condition, lower extremity stiffness in the NEm condition differed significantly from both the PE (p = 0.033) and NEg (p = 0.022) conditions, while hip energy absorption in the NEm condition differed significantly only from the NEg condition (p = 0.038). Additionally, within the NEm condition, hip energy absorption was significantly greater during dual-task landing than during single-task landing (p = 0.039). Dual-tasking elicits a more rigid landing strategy in individuals with FAI, marked by elevated knee stiffness and reduced hip flexion. Emotional priming further modulates these dual-task-related biomechanical alterations. Compared with the NEm condition, both PE and NEg conditions attenuated selected indicators of landing rigidity; the PE condition additionally decreased peak VGRF, whereas the NEg condition reduced hip energy absorption. These effects appeared to occur through distinct biomechanical pathways, with PE primarily influencing impact loading and NEg influencing proximal mechanical contribution. These findings provide preliminary evidence that emotional modulation may influence landing biomechanics under cognitive load and may have implications for injury prevention strategies in individuals with FAI.

records.title: Learned helplessness is associated with jump-landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
records.abstract: Persistent biomechanical alterations following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) contribute to reduced functional performance, increased reinjury risk, and diminished joint health. Rehabilitation emphasizes strength and functional restoration; however, neurobehavioral adaptations may persist. Learned helplessness, characterized by reduced motivation, maladaptive biomechanics, and learned non-use of the reconstructed limb, may relate to post-operative neuromuscular control. However, its relationship with dynamic movement after ACLR remains unclear. This study examined the association between learned helplessness and bilateral lower extremity kinematics during jump-landings in individuals following ACLR. Thirty-three individuals with primary, unilateral ACLR completed a learned helplessness scale and jump-landing task with three-dimensional lower-extremity kinematics. Sagittal and frontal plane knee and hip angles were assessed at initial contact and peak landing. Correlations and regression analyses examined associations with learned helplessness, controlling for age, sex, and time since surgery. Participants were 2.78 ± 2.78 years post-ACLR and demonstrated low helplessness scores. Greater learned helplessness was moderately associated with greater peak knee abduction in the ACLR limb (r = 0.564, p = 0.001). Weak associations were also observed with reduced peak hip flexion in the ACLR (r = -0.370, p = 0.048) and contralateral limbs (r = -0.415, p = 0.025), which did not survive sensitivity analyses. Learned helplessness was independently associated with greater peak knee abduction angle in the ACLR limb (B = 0.230, p = 0.007). The overall model accounted for 34.8% of the variance in peak knee abduction. Learned helplessness appears to be associated with frontal plane knee mechanics following ACLR. Consideration of psychological and neurobehavioral constructs in rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment following ACLR is important.

records.title: Literature Review of the Utility of Ultrasound for Adolescent and Child Ankle Injuries.
records.abstract: Pediatric posterior ankle pain is a common and challenging presentation due to the complex anatomy and a broad differential diagnosis that includes apophysitis, tendon injuries, fractures, impingement syndromes, infection, and inflammatory arthropathies. Initial evaluation typically consists of physical examination and radiographs, which are often inconclusive and may result in delayed diagnosis, repeat imaging, and/or prolonged immobilization. Magnetic resonance imaging is the gold standard for most of these injuries, but it is expensive and logistically difficult for the pediatric population. A rapid, accessible, and cost-effective imaging modality is needed to improve early detection and management. This review evaluates the role of ultrasound in assessing posterior ankle pathology in pediatric patients. Ultrasound demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy in identifying Achilles tendon tears and differentiating partial- from full-thickness injuries while also assisting in treatment decision making through dynamic tendon gap assessment. It is recommended in several studies for evaluating Achilles tendinopathy and may have predictive value for future symptoms. Emerging evidence supports its adjunctive role in Sever disease and posterior ankle impingement syndrome as well. For osseous and infectious conditions, ultrasound can identify findings suggestive of calcaneal stress fractures, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Although magnetic resonance imaging remains the gold standard for these diagnoses, ultrasound improves the detection of joint effusions and synovitis and enhances the accuracy of diagnostic joint aspirations. Overall, ultrasound is a dynamic, radiation-free modality that serves as a powerful adjunctive tool in evaluating pediatric posterior ankle pain.

records.title: Long-term physical health needs of UK military veterans: evaluation of the Op RESTORE health navigation service.
records.abstract: The long-term physical health needs of UK veterans have not been well characterised. Veterans often present with physical health issues attributable to their time in service. Prior to 2016, no dedicated National Health Service (NHS) pathway existed to address these needs. Op RESTORE was established in 2016 to provide coordinated, specialist-led care for veterans with service-attributable physical health conditions. This study describes 10 years of service delivery. A retrospective cross-sectional observational analysis of prospectively collected registry data was performed (2016-2025). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and statistical comparisons performed against national datasets and between internal subcohorts. A total of 1794 referrals were recorded. Most patients were male Army veterans and presented a median of 15 years after military discharge. Most pathology was non-operational and only 11% of 487 veterans with a documented injury setting had injuries related to combat. Musculoskeletal pathology predominated (79% of 1081 with a confirmed pathway), particularly lower-limb (56%) and spinal injuries (31%). Obesity was highly prevalent (55% of 174 recorded body mass indexes), exceeding national age-matched rates. Mental health comorbidity was common (69%). 64% required navigation to a new clinical pathway. EQ-5D-5L scores improved significantly between referral and discharge from Op RESTORE (p<0.001). Veterans accessing Op RESTORE predominantly present with delayed, chronic musculoskeletal and pain-related morbidity rather than acute combat-related injury. The long interval between military discharge and Op RESTORE presentation highlights a poorly documented and insufficiently monitored progression of service-related pathology over time. This represents missed opportunities for early identification, prevention and intervention. The high burden of multimorbidity and frequent need for specialist triage indicate gaps in standard NHS referral pathways for veterans. Coordinated healthcare navigation addresses unmet need and, in uncontrolled analysis, was associated with improved quality of life. Improved characterisation and longitudinal monitoring of veteran physical health could inform targeted, preventive and integrated service models.

records.title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
records.abstract: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols. To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes. A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736). Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

records.title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
records.abstract: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height. Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations. Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006). Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research. Level III.

records.title: Minimally Invasive Surgery for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy Using a Double-Row SpeedBridge Repair with Rip-Stop Augmentation.
records.abstract: The present video article describes a minimally invasive surgery (MIS) technique utilizing a double-row rip-stop SpeedBridge (Arthrex) repair for the treatment of insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT). This procedure is utilized when nonoperative treatment has failed, with the goal of returning patients to their previous levels of activity while avoiding the complications associated with more open procedures. All products mentioned in the videos are manufactured by Arthrex. The surgical technique is performed with 4 small incisions-2 distal and 2 proximal. Any Haglund deformity and/or enthesophyte are resected with use of an MIS burr through the 2 distal portals. The central third of the Achilles tendon is partially detached with this resection and is repaired with use of a double-row repair. Proximal anchors are placed, and sutures are passed through the Achilles tendon. Working knotless sutures are tensioned to create a rip-stop suture. The sutures are passed and shuttled to the distal row, creating a double-row repair. The distal row is drilled and tapped. The double-row repair is completed with insertion of distal anchors under appropriate tension. Nonoperative treatment is beneficial in the initial stages of the condition and is successful in 60% to 80% of patients1-3. Initial treatment strategies for IAT include RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy. Eccentric exercise and extracorporeal shockwave therapy have shown promising results3. Paratendinous injections, such as with platelet-rich plasma, have shown various levels of success and need further evaluation3. When nonoperative treatment has failed, operative treatment is a viable option. The surgical approach should be chosen on a patient-specific basis, as different tendinopathy patterns and different associated osseous and soft-tissue conditions may influence preoperative planning. There are a variety of different surgical techniques that include open, endoscopic, and MIS procedures. This MIS technique utilizing a double-row SpeedBridge repair with rip-stop augmentation yields fewer wound complications, less pain, quicker initiation of rehabilitation protocols, and quicker return to sport compared with more invasive techniques. Furthermore, the addition of the rip-stop augment to the double-row SpeedBridge repair improves dynamic mechanical strength and mitigates suture tearing through the tendon4. In our experience, patients who undergo this technique will be weight-bearing in a controlled-ankle-motion boot immediately postoperatively and out of the boot by 6 weeks postoperatively, with progressive return to full activities as tolerated. Our study of 61 patients undergoing the double-row SpeedBridge repair demonstrated favorable outcomes, with Foot and Ankle Disability Index scores improving from a mean of 56.3 preoperatively to 98.62 at 12 months postoperatively and visual analog scale pain scores improving from a mean of 7.25 to 0.476. There were no postoperative ruptures at a mean follow-up of 12.5 months. Eleven patients had minor complications within 3 months, including 6 who reported some central numbness over the Achilles tendon6. We expect these outcomes to improve as surgeons become more comfortable and skilled performing MIS techniques. Proper patient selection (chronic IAT with Haglund deformity and/or an enthesophyte) will help ensure optimal outcomes.It is important to develop a subcutaneous plane for suture passage.The use of fluoroscopy or a nanoscope is helpful in ensuring that the proper bone is resected with the MIS burr.We have found that the irrigator from the MIS burr can be utilized alongside a Frazier suction tip to help remove excess bone.Suture management is important. Precisely maneuver the sutures at all times; it is very important that the sutures do not get tangled so that the procedure flows efficiently.Make sure to fully tension both sutures in order to place the ripstop.
