records.title: Multimodal Gait Acquisition and Musculoskeletal Simulation for Subject-Specific Evaluation of Ankle Exosuit Cable Anchor Positioning in Cerebral Palsy.
records.abstract: Wearable ankle exosuits require precise evaluation frameworks to optimize assistive force transmission and subject-specific configuration. This study presents a multimodal sensor-based experimental and computational framework to assess the influence of ankle exosuit cable anchor positioning on neuromuscular and energetic responses during gait in a child with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy. Three-dimensional kinematics were acquired using an optical motion capture system (12 infrared cameras), while ground reaction forces were recorded through instrumented force plates. Metabolic cost was experimentally measured using portable respiratory gas analysis. These sensor-derived data were integrated into a participant-scaled musculoskeletal model in OpenSim to simulate nine cable anchor configurations and quantify changes in muscle activation, force production, mechanical impulse, and metabolic power. Cable geometry altered the predicted distribution of plantar-flexor loading across configurations. Experimental measurements were not available for muscle-level outputs or for the assisted configurations; therefore, these responses were interpreted as model-derived, exploratory comparisons rather than experimentally validated physiological effects. Configurations with larger offsets from the heel-reference position tended to yield greater reductions in gastrocnemius demand, whereas configurations nearer the heel reference more effectively reduced soleus loading but increased secondary stabilizing muscle recruitment. Predicted metabolic changes across assisted configurations ranged from a 0.86% reduction to a 6.28% increase relative to the experimental baseline, and from a 2.66% reduction to a 4.33% increase relative to the simulated non-actuated condition. These differences should be interpreted as indicators of model sensitivity rather than demonstrated energetic improvements. This study demonstrates how multimodal gait sensing combined with musculoskeletal simulation provides a quantitative tool for preliminary screening of cable-driven ankle exosuit design in pathological gait.

records.title: Musculoskeletal Complaint Patterns and Training Impact in Adult Triathletes During the 2023 Season.
records.abstract: Objectives: To characterize self-report musculoskeletal complaints, anatomical distribution, healthcare utilization, training impact, and associations with demographic and training characteristics among adult triathletes during the 2023 season. Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional survey was conducted among community-based triathletes recruited through social media and triathlon organizations. Adults aged ≥18 years who completed or intended to complete at least one triathlon in 2023 were included (N = 245). Demographic characteristics, years of participation, race focus, and weekly training volume were collected. Main outcomes included self-reported musculoskeletal complaints, anatomical location, complaint classification, healthcare utilization, and training disruption. Results: Of 245 participants (60.0% male; most frequent age group 30-34 years), 127 of 242 with available complaint data (52.5%) reported at least one complaint, totaling 175 reported complaints. The lower extremity accounted for 79.4% of complaints, most commonly the hip/pelvis (22.3%), lower leg (18.7%), knee (17.3%), ankle (15.1%), and foot/toes (15.1%). Running was the most frequently reported activity associated with complaint onset (61%). The number of reported complaints was not significantly associated with the broad demographic or training characteristics examined. Healthcare utilization was reported for 62.4% of complaints with available healthcare data. Among complaints with available training impact data, 50.6% resulted in both missed and modified training, 28.2% in modified training only, and 21.2% in missed training only. Conclusions: More than half of the triathletes surveyed reported musculoskeletal complaints during the 2023 season, with lower-extremity and overuse complaints predominating and running most frequently associated with complaint onset. Broad demographic and general training characteristics were not significantly associated with the number of reported complaints. These findings highlight the burden and training consequences of self-reported musculoskeletal complaints among adult triathletes and support the need for prospective surveillance incorporating discipline-specific exposure and more detailed training load measures.

records.title: Musculoskeletal Findings Following Pre-Participation Screening in Young Athletes: A Retrospective Observational Study.
records.abstract: Background: Pre-participation screening (PPS) is widely used to evaluate athletes before sport participation, traditionally focusing on cardiovascular risk prevention. However, musculoskeletal assessment performed during PPS may also allow early identification of biomechanical and structural abnormalities that can affect sport participation during growth. Objectives: This study aimed to describe the prevalence, clinical characteristics, and management pathways of musculoskeletal alterations detected during PPS in young athletes, with particular focus on referral patterns to pediatric Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) specialists. Methods: This retrospective observational study included athletes aged ≤15 years who underwent PPS between January 2022 and December 2023 at the Sports Medicine Unit of Noale (ULSS 3 Serenissima, Venice, Italy). Musculoskeletal screening was systematically performed during PPS. Athletes presenting newly detected abnormalities were either managed conservatively by the sports physician or referred for PM&R evaluation. Clinical indications for referral, imaging investigations, diagnoses, and treatment strategies were analyzed. Results: A total of 707 athletes underwent PPS during the study period. After applying exclusion criteria, 635 athletes were eligible for analysis. Musculoskeletal alterations were identified in 141 athletes (22.2%). Among them, 54 athletes were referred for PM&R evaluation and 40 completed the consultation. No statistically significant differences were observed between referred and non-referred athletes. The most frequent reasons for referral were suspected scoliosis (n = 22), foot alignment disorders n = 18), thoracic hyperkyphosis (n = 5), and lower limb length discrepancy (n = 4). Specialist evaluation resulted in conservative management in most cases, including corrective exercise programs and orthotic interventions, while one athlete required surgical treatment for congenital scoliosis. Conclusions: Musculoskeletal screening during PPS identified a broad spectrum of findings in young athletes, including clinically relevant abnormalities requiring specialist evaluation and management. These findings suggest that musculoskeletal assessment may provide an opportunity for early clinical identification within PPS; however, prospective studies are needed to evaluate diagnostic accuracy, long-term clinical benefit, injury prevention, and cost-effectiveness before routine implementation can be recommended.

records.title: Musical Feedback to Reduce the Knee Adduction Moment Via Center of Pressure Medialization: A Proof-of-Concept Study in Healthy Adults for Knee Osteoarthritis Gait Retraining.
records.abstract: Elevated knee adduction moment (KAM) is a primary contributor to medial knee osteoarthritis (OA) progression. Medialization of center of pressure (CoP) can reduce KAM, but sustaining engagement and a consistent walking pattern remains a challenge. We investigated whether concurrent plantar pressure-modulated musical feedback would cue a medial CoP shift to reduce KAM without producing detrimental lower limb compensations in healthy adults. Twelve participants (6F/6M; age: 31.5 ± 5.3 years) walked while a marker-based motion analysis system (Qualisys) and wireless pressure-sensing insoles (Moticon) recorded gait. Real-time insole data drove auditory feedback: self-selected music was progressively muffled whenever the participant failed to shift their CoP medially beyond their threshold (25 % reduction in peak lateral CoP from baseline). Gait was assessed at baseline, post-instructions, and post-training. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used for kinetics and spatiotemporal outcomes, and statistical parametric mapping, as a secondary analysis, for kinematic waveforms. All participants medialized their CoP based on instructions and musical feedback. Musical feedback significantly reduced the second KAM peak (post-training: -13.7 %; p = 0.002) and the knee adduction angular impulse (post-training: -9.4 %; p < 0.001), but with a borderline increase in peak knee flexion moment (p = 0.050) that may reflect compensation. Gait adaptations were executed without a change in walking speed. Also, foot progression angle and stride width remained unchanged. CoP medialization was achieved mainly through ankle inversion, ankle external rotation, and hip internal rotation. These preliminary findings support concurrent sonified biofeedback for gait retraining, warranting evaluation in medial knee OA patients.

records.title: Nationwide Trends, Regional Variation and Seasonality of Surgically Treated Achilles Tendon Rupture in Japan: An Analysis of Descriptive Epidemiological Study.
records.abstract: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a common foot and ankle injury among physically active adults. Nationwide evidence on long-term trends, regional variation, seasonality and COVID-19-related changes in Japan is limited. We characterised the surgical burden of ATR using a national administrative database. We conducted a nationwide descriptive epidemiological study using aggregated data from the National Database of Health Insurance Claims and Specific Health Checkups (NDB) Open Data for fiscal years (FY) 2014-2022. Temporal trends, prefectural variation, seasonal patterns and pandemic-associated changes were examined using counts, population-based rates and quasi-Poisson regression. During FY2014-2019, approximately 11,200 surgeries were performed annually (8.8 per 100,000 person). In FY2020, incidence declined to 5.9 per 100,000 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.67), with greater reductions among adults aged 30-59 (61%-64% of baseline) and, after age adjustment, among women (IRR 0.61 vs. 0.71 in men; interaction p = 0.039). Incidence partially recovered in FY2021-2022 (7.6 per 100,000; IRR 0.86). Incidence varied across the 47 prefectures (pre-COVID range: 5.0-16.7 per 100,000), and all declined in FY2020 (mean ratio 0.69). Monthly counts peaked in spring-early summer and were higher in spring than in winter (p = 0.018). The incidence of surgically treated ATR in Japan was stable before the COVID-19 pandemic, declined markedly in FY2020 and partially recovered thereafter, with the largest reductions among working-age adults and women. Regional variation and seasonality were preserved. These findings can inform surgical and rehabilitation service planning.

records.title: Optimal Wearing Position of Accelerometers for Monitoring Energy Expenditure in Tennis.
records.abstract: Monitoring energy expenditure (EE) in tennis is complicated by its intermittent and technically variable movements. This study identified the optimal accelerometer wearing position for EE prediction and examined the contribution of additional covariates. Thirty-eight right-handed national second-class tennis players (11 females, 27 males) performed 4 tennis-specific technical movements with accelerometers worn at 9 positions. Criterion EE was measured using Metamax3B portable metabolic analyzer. Associations of accelerometer-derived variables with criterion EE were examined through Pearson or Spearman correlation analyses. Candidate covariates were screened using Akaike information criterion-based backward selection. Three linear mixed-effects models were evaluated per position with participant as a random intercept. Variance inflation factors, leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and Bland-Altman analyses assessed multicollinearity, predictive performance, and agreement, respectively. Lower-back and ankle positions showed more frequent significant correlations with criterion EE. Backward selection retained heart rate, basal metabolic rate, sex, and movement type across positions; all primary-model variance inflation factors were below 3. Across the 3 models, marginal Rm2 of lower back ranked first (.787) and of the dominant-side ankle second (.749). In primary models, lower back had the lowest cross-validated root mean square error (.810). Bland-Altman mean differences were close to zero in top-performing models, while proportional-bias slopes were significantly negative at all positions. Lower back represents the optimal accelerometer placement for model-based EE monitoring in tennis, and incorporating participant variables and movement type enhances prediction accuracy. These findings support sport-specific sensor placement and individualized calibration strategies to improve training load monitoring and nutritional planning.

records.title: Outcomes of a Multidisciplinary Lower Limb Fracture Care Pathway in a Tertiary Hospital: A 3-Year Experience of 1073 Geriatric Patients.
records.abstract: Geriatric lower limb fractures place a significant burden on tertiary healthcare systems. This study evaluates the outcomes of a fast-track, multidisciplinary lower limb fracture care pathway implemented at a tertiary hospital in Singapore. This study aims to describe and compare the functional outcomes, mortality, and the comparative impact of time to surgery (TTS) across different geriatric lower limb fractures (knee, femur shaft, and ankle) within the pathway, using hip fractures as a benchmark. A retrospective cohort study was conducted of patients ≥ 65 years old with non-pathological, surgically-treated lower limb fractures admitted to a tertiary institution between December 2020 and April 2024. Primary outcomes included postoperative functional status assessed via Modified Barthel Index (MBI) scores and perioperative complications, while the secondary outcome was 12-month mortality. Multivariate regression analyses evaluated predictors influencing these outcomes. The cohort predominantly consisted of hip fracture patients (82.2%), with knee (7.3%), ankle (5.4%), and femur shaft (5.1%) fractures comprising smaller groups. At 12 months, there were no significant differences in mortality across fracture types (overall mortality: 7.2%). Functional outcomes, measured by MBI scores, showed significant improvement over 12 months, with no significant difference between fracture types (p = 0.32). Multivariate analysis identified younger age, female gender, higher pre-fracture MBI scores, and lower clinical frailty scores as positive predictors of 12-month functional outcomes. Early surgery (< 48 h) was significantly associated with better 12-month functional outcomes in knee fracture patients. TTS (< 48 h) significantly influenced mortality outcomes in hip fractures only. These findings describe comparable functional outcomes and mortality across fracture types and outcomes observed for a broader range of lower limb injuries beyond hip fractures are favorable under a coordinated multidisciplinary care pathway.

records.title: Outcomes of open and endoscopic excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in athletes: a systematic review with exploratory analysis of prognostic factors.
records.abstract: A symptomatic os trigonum causes posterior ankle impingement in athletes and is excised when conservative treatment fails. Previous syntheses have pooled mean outcomes across mixed populations, and poor outcomes have not been defined consistently. Six databases were searched for open or endoscopic os trigonum excision in athletes, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Techniques were compared within comparative studies, with supplementary pooling. A composite poor-outcome profile and eight candidate factors were examined at study-arm level. Thirteen studies (17 arms, 440 participants) were included. Failure to return to prior level was uncommon (9 of 438; 0-6.2% by arm). In the randomised trial, return to prior sport level was 4.4 weeks faster after endoscopic excision (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-6.1); pooling two further non-randomised studies with imputed SDs gave 4.9 weeks (95% CI 3.3-6.6). Trial complications occurred in 1 of 26 endoscopic and 6 of 26 open patients (odds ratio 7.50, 95% CI 0.83-67.49); the two-study pooled odds ratio was 5.59 (95% CI 1.10-28.35) from 10 events. Both nerve injuries described as permanent followed open surgery. The composite depended on arm size and threshold choice, and five of eight candidate factors could not be tested. Poor outcomes are uncommon after either approach. Low-certainty evidence suggests faster return to sport after endoscopic excision; complication evidence is of very low certainty, though no nerve injury described as permanent followed endoscopic excision. A consensus definition of return to sport is needed.

records.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes Plateau at 1 Year Compared With 2 Years After Open Proximal Hamstring Repair.
records.abstract: To determine whether there is a significant difference between 1- and 2-year postoperative patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) after proximal hamstring repair (PHR). This retrospective study used data from an institutional registry of patients who underwent PHR between October 2021 and December 2023 with a minimum follow-up of 24 months. Patients who completed preoperative and 1- and 2-year postoperative surveys were included in this study. PROMs included the Lower Extremity Functional Scale, the Hip Outcome Score, the Perth Hamstring Assessment, and the 12-Item Short Form Survey. Cohort-specific minimal clinically important difference was calculated. Return to sport and surgical satisfaction were included as secondary outcomes. Univariate analyses compared clinical outcomes. Sixty-two of 84 eligible patients met the inclusion criteria for this study, with a mean follow-up time of 23.2 months (range 22.4-24.8). No significant differences were found between 1- and 2-year PROMs after PHR (P > .05). There were no statistically significant differences in the proportion of patients who achieved minimal clinically important difference at 1 year versus 2 years postoperatively, and these differences remained nonsignificant after disaggregating the data by sex (P > .05). After 1 year postoperatively, there were no significant additional improvements in the ability to return to sport (P = .371), sport level (P > .99), or percentage of return to sport (P = .961). No significant differences were found between 1- and 2-year PROMs after PHR. PROM scores, minimal clinically important difference achievement rates, return to sport, and surgical satisfaction outcomes were stable from 1 to 2 years postoperatively, with no clinically meaningful improvements observed in the second postoperative year. Level IV, retrospective case series.

records.title: Physical Examination of Chronic Ankle Instability: Current Concepts.
records.abstract: Chronic ankle instability is a common condition with a substantial public health burden. When non-operative treatment fails, surgery should address both the ligament injury and associated lesions. Their identification relies on a comprehensive physical examination, which remains challenging and has limited reproducibility. This narrative Current Concepts review summarizes the mechanical and structural physical examination findings, the clinical tests used to assess the lateral ligament complex, medial ligamentous structures, the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, the subtalar joint, associated impingement lesions, and generalized joint hypermobility, that inform surgical planning. For the lateral ligament complex, the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests demonstrate high specificity but limited sensitivity. Modified maneuvers, including the anterolateral and reverse anterolateral drawer tests, may improve diagnostic accuracy. However, reported reliability and accuracy remain inconsistent, and no single test is both highly sensitive and specific, supporting a bilateral, comparative, multi-test examination. A secondary aim of this review is to evaluate how patient positioning influences examination feasibility. No single position enables complete assessment, and comparative reliability studies are lacking. Based on biomechanical rationale and clinical experience rather than comparative evidence, the prone position may offer practical advantages, allowing a lateral ankle view and isolated subtalar assessment, but these potential advantages have not been confirmed by comparative studies. Current best practice remains a systematic, bilateral examination using complementary tests while recognizing the limitations of each maneuver.

records.title: Positioning and Traction Application Technique in Patient with Below Knee Amputation Using the Patients Own Prosthesis for Intertrochanteric Femur Fracture Fixation Surgery: A Case Report with Review of Literature.
records.abstract: Surgical fixation of an intertrochanteric femur fracture in a patient with a below-knee amputation (BKA) is a challenging scenario for the orthopedic surgeon. Applying traction to reduce the fracture and maintaining it until definitive fixation is done with an implant is difficult, because the shortened limb cannot be secured to the foot attachment of a standard fracture table. Reported techniques are either invasive, requiring pins or wires, or need additional equipment. We describe a non-invasive alternative and discuss the various techniques available to address this problem. A 69-year-old woman with a right BKA presented with right hip pain and inability to bear weight following a fall at home. Before injury, she was independently ambulatory using a prosthesis. The stump was healthy and well healed. Radiographs revealed an intertrochanteric femur fracture with varus angulation. Closed reduction and internal fixation using a proximal femoral nail was planned. The prosthesis was secured to the stump using its velcro straps, additional bandages, and adhesive tapes and attached to the fracture table in the routine manner. Gradual traction was applied with internal rotation of the foot, and reduction was confirmed fluoroscopically. Fixation was performed using an 11 × 240 mm PFN with a 135° neck-shaft angle. Post-operative radiographs showed satisfactory alignment and stable fixation. She mobilized non-weight-bearing with a walker on post-operative day 1 and resumed full weight-bearing using the prosthesis at one month. Six-month follow-up demonstrated satisfactory radiological and functional outcomes. Using the patient's own BK prosthesis for positioning, traction, and rotational control effectively achieved and maintained the lower limb traction required during surgery. It allowed satisfactory reduction and stable fixation while avoiding invasive procedures or soft-tissue complications, and is simple, available, and cost-effective because it relies on a device the patient already uses. It adds a non-invasive option to the reduction methods available for hip fractures in amputees.

records.title: Post-Treatment Follow-up, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport: Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle.
records.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and return to sport (RTS) are key components of recovery following surgical management of osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). However, substantial variability exists in postoperative protocols, with limited high-quality evidence guiding clinical practicesMethodsInternational experts convened during the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) in Pittsburgh, USA (2017), with subsequent ratification of recommendations in New York, USA (2025). The original consensus statements were developed using a modified Delphi process involving electronic surveys, structured questionnaires, and expert discussion. Consensus strength was defined as consensus (51%-74%), strong consensus (75%-99%), or unanimous (100%). The recommendations addressed postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following OLT management.ResultsA total of 16 consensus statements were developed and subsequently ratified, comprising 7 statements addressing post-treatment follow-up and 9 addressing rehabilitation and RTS. All statements achieved strong consensus, with agreement ranging from 75% to 98%. Follow-up recommendations emphasized standardized clinical assessment and patient-reported outcomes, with extended monitoring in select patients. Rehabilitation recommendations supported early controlled motion and progressive weightbearing, with individualized progression according to procedure and clinical performance. Return to sport recommendations emphasized functional recovery and individualized decision-making. Ten statements (63%) were classified exclusively as Grade E, highlighting the limited evidence supporting several recommendations.ConclusionThe ICCRA consensus statements establish a structured framework for postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following surgical management of OLT. Despite strong expert agreement, several recommendations remain supported by limited evidence, underlining the need for prospective studies to establish validated, procedure-specific rehabilitation protocols and objective RTS criteria.Level of Evidence:V, expert consensus.

records.title: Preseason Deceleration Index Is Lower in Collegiate Football Athletes Who Sustain Time-Loss Lower-Quarter Injuries: A Three-Season Prospective Cohort Study.
records.abstract: Deceleration capacity is a fundamental yet underappreciated component of multidirectional sport performance. Non-contact lower-quarter injuries frequently occur during rapid deceleration and change-of-direction tasks, yet braking capacity remains under-evaluated relative to acceleration and speed. The Deceleration Index (DI) has been proposed as a ratio-based metric of peak deceleration to peak acceleration. Hypothesis/Purpose: The purpose of this study was to compare preseason Deceleration Index values between collegiate football athletes who sustained a time-loss lower-quarter injury and position-matched uninjured athletes across three competitive seasons. It was hypothesized that football athletes who sustain a non-contact time-loss lower-quarter injury would demonstrate lower preseason DI values than position-matched uninjured athletes. Prospective cohort study. Division I male collegiate football athletes completed preseason change-of-direction testing (5-10-5 test) during summer training camp at the beginning of each season. Following a warmup, data were captured using a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) integrated with an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). The DI was calculated as peak deceleration value divided by peak acceleration value. Athletes were prospectively followed three consecutive seasons for time-loss lower-quarter injuries. Injured athletes (n = 57) were matched 1:1 by playing position to uninjured controls (n = 57). Independent-samples t-tests compared group means, with Cohen's d for effect size. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed within-sample discriminatory ability. Injured and uninjured athletes were similar at baseline in age (mean 22 years in each group), height, body mass, and BMI (all p ≥ 0.09). Injured athletes demonstrated significantly lower preseason DI than uninjured athletes (0.90 ± 0.07 vs 1.10 ± 0.10; p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 2.30). ROC analysis showed excellent within-sample discrimination (AUC = 0.96, 95% CI 0.89-0.99); a DI ≤ 1.00 yielded a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity of 91%. Lower preseason DI values were associated with subsequent non-contact time-loss lower-quarter injury in collegiate football athletes. DI may serve as a practical field-based risk indicator reflecting braking capacity relative to acceleration; causal inference and the proposed threshold require independent validation. 2b (individual prospective cohort study).

records.title: Prior Lower Extremity Injury as a Risk Factor for Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Soccer Players.
records.abstract: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a serious injury in professional soccer, often leading to prolonged absence, diminished performance, and increased risk of reinjury. While ATR epidemiology and biomechanics have been extensively studied, the contribution of previous lower-extremity injuries to rupture risk remains incompletely characterized. Given the integrated nature of the kinetic chain, we hypothesized that players with previous injuries to related structures would be disproportionately represented among those sustaining ATR. Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3. Injury data were obtained from Transfermark. Professional soccer players with complete ATR from 2001 to 2025 were identified. Previous injuries were categorized into anatomical groups. Players with documented histories were compared with an injured, non-ATR reference population. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous time-loss data as means ± standard deviations and medians. Between-group injury risks were quantified using risk ratios. Data aggregation and statistical calculations were conducted in Python. A total of 1362 ATR cases were identified from 1,073,633 players, of whom 750 (55.1%) had previous injuries. Among these, the most frequent antecedent pathologies involved the knee (37.9%), thigh (34.5%), and hip/groin (27.9%), followed by ankle (23.6%), Achilles tendon (14.3%), foot (11.9%), and calf (10.8%). Compared with controls, ATR players exhibited higher rates of previous Achilles injuries (107/750 [14.3%] vs 1350/50,000 [2.7%]; 5.3-fold increase; P < .001), thigh injuries (259/750 [34.5%] vs 7600/50,000 [15.2%]; 2.3-fold increase; P < .001), and hip/groin injuries (209/750 [27.9%] vs 6900/50,000 [13.8%]; 2-fold increase; P < .001). Previous Achilles and foot injuries were associated with the longest mean absences (71.5 ± 92.6 days and 60.2 ± 60.9 days, respectively), which were significantly longer than absences from other previous injury types (Kruskal-Wallis P < .001; Mann-Whitney U tests for Achilles vs others: P < .01). This large-scale analysis demonstrates that ATR is rarely an isolated event, with more than half of cases preceded by lower-extremity injuries. The overrepresentation of Achilles, thigh, and foot pathology may support the concept of cumulative injury progression and highlights potential biomechanical links contributing to rupture.

records.title: Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of a Sock-Based Plantar Strain Sensing System for Diabetic Foot Monitoring.
records.abstract: Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFUs) pose a serious health risk to people with diabetes, with a high risk of recurrence following the first DFU and a risk of foot amputation or death. It greatly impacts patient quality of life and costs the NHS up to 0.7% of its annual budget. Over the last 20 years, work has highlighted the link between DFU formation and normal forces. More recently, work has highlighted the importance of strain/shear forces, which are inherently coupled with normal forces. While limited lab-based in-shoe systems have been produced to detect shear, they alter the shoe-foot interface and are not commercially available. Additionally, consultation with people with diabetes highlighted that they may not wear shoes around the house, leaving long periods where in-shoe solutions cannot track forces. We, therefore, present the development of a novel plantar shear measuring system, the Shear Tracking for Enhanced Prevention Sock (STEPS), an instrumented garment to provide an accessible tool for people at risk of DFUs. Integrating sensors within the sock provides a solution that seamlessly integrates within the foot-shoe environment, is suitable for shoeless use, and helps mitigate adherence issues. A prototype STEPS was produced, successfully integrating printed resistive strain sensors (proxy for shear) within custom-designed socks with flexible connectivity to a welt-mounted data acquisition unit. Proof-of-concept testing characterised the system's ability to measure plantar strain. A single-participant pilot study demonstrated that STEPS captures repeatable, gait-synchronised strain signals during walking, with a stationary noise floor below 10% of the typical per-cycle resistance response and between-repeat correlations of R = 0.41 and 0.78 for Sensor 1 and 2 respectively, supporting its potential to detect strain (as proxy for shear) during daily activity.

records.title: Relationship between global functional outcomes and patient-reported instability after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction: A midterm case series of 292 patients.
records.abstract: To evaluate midterm patient-reported outcomes, return to sport (RTS) rates and instability-specific symptoms after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction (AALALR), and to evaluate the relationship between global functional recovery and perceived ankle stability. We retrospectively analysed 292 patients who underwent AALALR between January 2015 and May 2022, with a mean follow-up of 4.9 ± 1.8 years. Global outcomes were assessed using the foot and ankle ability measure (FAAM) and simple ankle value (SAV), while instability-specific perception was evaluated with the French Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT-F). RTS, satisfaction and complications were also recorded. No objective postoperative laxity assessment was performed. Mean FAAM-ADL was 94.3 ± 12.0, FAAM-Sports 87.5 ± 20.4 and SAV 85.1 ± 17.4; 89.7% of patients returned to sport and 91.1% were satisfied. Overall, 104 patients (35.6%; 95% CI, 30.3-41.3) met the CAIT-F criterion for instability at follow-up (score ≤23/30). Patients with CAIT-F-defined instability had significantly lower FAAM and SAV scores and RTS rates (all p < 0.001), although most had returned to sport (79.8%) and were satisfied (81.7%). The CAIT-F correlated moderately with FAAM-activities of daily living (ADL), FAAM-Sports and SAV (Spearman ρ = 0.68-0.69) and receiver operating characteristic analysis showed imperfect agreement between global scores and CAIT-F-defined categories (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.82-0.85). The reoperation rate was 5.5%. AALALR provides high midterm satisfaction, favourable functional scores and favourable RTS rates. However, over one-third of patients reported current CAIT-F-defined instability symptoms. Global and instability-specific instruments are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable, and prospective studies including objective laxity assessment are needed. Level IV, case series.

records.title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
records.abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

records.title: Return to Sport After Foot and Ankle Surgery Is Inconsistently Defined and Assessed: A Systematic Review.
records.abstract: To conduct a systematic review of return-to-sport (RTS) definitions in the orthopaedic literature, addressing common operative athletic foot and ankle pathologies including ankle instability, Achilles tendon ruptures or tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fractures. A systematic review was performed in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Cochrane, Embase, Medline, and CINAHL databases were searched for studies published through March 2024. Inclusion criteria were studies in which subjects were involved in some level of sports and received surgery for 1 of 3 common sports-related injuries: ankle instability, Achilles tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fracture. The primary outcome was each study's definition of RTS. There were 145 articles that met all inclusion criteria. Of these, 73 articles investigated ankle instability, 56 investigated Achilles tendinopathy, and 16 investigated fifth metatarsal fracture. Seventy-nine articles (54.5%) had an unclear definition of RTS with 66 articles (45.5%) reporting a precise definition. Sixty-four articles (44.1%) provided an isolated binary metric reporting whether a patient returned to sport or failed to provide a method for determining the timepoint for RTS. Thirty-eight (26.2%) of the articles used an objective start criterion (e.g., resumption of competition), followed by custom (n = 27, 18.6%) and standardized patient-reported questionnaire use (n = 21, 14.5%). Most articles included in this systematic review did not provide an explicit definition of RTS or a clearly defined assessment methodology. When specified, RTS was assessed using objective events, custom questionnaires, or standardized patient-reported outcome measures, highlighting substantial heterogeneity in both RTS definitions and assessment approaches across foot and ankle literature. Level IV, systematic review of Level I to IV studies.

records.title: Return to sport and clinical outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes.
records.abstract: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) can compromise athletic performance and delay return to competition. Although primary ligament repair and ligament reconstruction are valid surgical options, comparative data remains limited. The primary aim was to evaluate overall return-to-sport outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes. The secondary aim was to compare return-to-sport and postoperative clinical outcomes between direct ligament repair and ligament reconstruction. Comparative retrospective study METHODS: This comparative cohort study included 54 athletes who underwent surgical stabilization for CAI between 2018 and 2024. Surgical procedures were categorized as primary repair and ligament reconstruction. The primary outcomes were RTS status and time to RTS. Secondary outcomes included postoperative Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores and residual complaints. The mean age was 25.6 ± 6.9 years, and 48% of patients were football players. The median interval from the latest injury to surgery was 6.0 months. RTS status was available for 49 of the 54 athletes (91%). Of these, 48 (98%) returned to sport at a mean time of 5.3 months (range 2.0 to 16.0), while one athlete did not return to sport. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with mean FAAM activities of daily living and sport scores of 96.2 ± 8.3 and 89.7 ± 20.4, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed among surgical groups in RTS status, time to RTS, FAAM scores, or residual complaints. Surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability was associated with favorable postoperative scores and a high RTS rate among athletes with available outcome data. The sample size and overall study design preclude conclusions regarding the equivalence or superiority of repair versus reconstruction.

records.title: Return to Sport and Risk Factors for Recurrence After Arthroscopic Anatomic Lateral Ankle Ligament Reconstruction.
records.abstract: Chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) often requires surgical stabilization when conservative management or primary repair fails. While arthroscopic anatomic reconstruction using tendon autograft is increasingly used, data on strict return-to-sport (RTS) metrics and risk factors for recurrence in high-demand populations remain limited. To evaluate the rate and timing of RTS, functional outcomes, and factors associated with failure after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction using a gracilis autograft. Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3. A total of 101 patients undergoing arthroscopic anatomic reconstruction with gracilis autograft for CLAI were evaluated at a minimum follow-up of 2 years. The primary outcome was RTS, defined as the resumption of full athletic activity. Secondary outcomes included return to preinjury level, recurrence of instability, rerupture, and functional assessment using the Foot and Ankle Outcome and Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores. Risk factors for failure to RTS and recurrence were analyzed using univariate regression and multivariate stepwise logistic regression. The overall RTS rate was 71.1% at a median delay of 6 months (5-8.5 months). However, only 45.6% of patients returned to their specific preinjury level. Multivariable analysis identified elevated body mass index (BMI) (P = .014) as an independent factor associated with failure to return to the preinjury level, while higher preoperative FAAM-Activities of Daily Living scores (P = .002) were factors associated with success. Significant improvements were observed in all functional scores at the final follow-up (P < .001). A confirmed recurrence of instability occurred in 11.9% of patients, comprising 9.9% (10/101) with ankle sprains and only 2% (2/101) with graft rupture. In univariate analysis, younger age (P = .007) and participation in pivot-contact sports (P = .040) were associated with recurrent instability. In multivariable analysis, younger age emerged as an independent factor associated with recurrent instability (P = .040). Arthroscopic anatomic reconstruction provided significant functional improvement with a low graft rupture rate (2%). However, returning to the preinjury level proved challenging (45.6%), particularly for patients with lower preoperative function or elevated BMI. Younger age was identified as an independent risk factor for recurrent sprains.

records.title: Severe injuries in competitive cycling during an olympic cycle: injury patterns, time loss, and return-to-performance outcomes.
records.abstract: Cycling is an established Olympic sport associated with a distinct injury profile that has not yet been comprehensively investigated. This study aimed to retrospectively assess and analyze severe cycling-related injuries resulting in ≥ 3 weeks of time loss over a complete Olympic cycle. A total of 192 cyclists were included, based on a retrospective online questionnaire assessing injury location, type, context, time loss, and return-to-sport outcomes. Comparisons by sex, discipline, and competitive level were performed at the athlete level using exact tests with 95% confidence intervals and were considered exploratory. Seventy-two of 192 athletes sustained at least one severe injury over the five-year period, corresponding to a proportion of 37.5% (95% CI 31.0-44.5). A total of 237 injuries were recorded, with the upper extremity (33.8%) and lower extremity (27.8%) being the most frequently affected regions. The most common diagnoses were hand fractures (n = 14), clavicle fractures (n = 13), and non-specific knee injuries (n = 9). Hand fractures (33.3%; p = 0.002) and shoulder dislocations (20.0%; p = 0.002) were most frequent among BMX athletes, while hand fractures also occurred more frequently in competitive athletes than in recreational athletes (13.5% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.001). Clavicle fractures occurred predominantly during competition and non-specific knee injuries during training. Mean time loss ranged from 6.5 weeks for hand fractures to 13.3 weeks for shoulder dislocations. Full return to pre-injury performance ranged from 85.7% after hand fractures to 28.6% after acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations. Injury patterns differed by discipline and setting, suggesting that prevention strategies should address both. The low rate of full return to performance after AC joint separations despite moderate time loss underlines the importance of distinguishing return to sport from return to performance in rehabilitation.

records.title: Sex-Equitable Machine Learning Prediction of Ankle Reinjury in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability: A 2-Year Prospective Cohort Study with Fairness Audit.
records.abstract: Patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) face a 2-year reinjury rate approaching 50%, but individualized prediction models that quantify which baseline impairments predict subsequent reinjury within an established CAI cohort remain scarce, and existing prediction models for ankle injury have not assessed sex-related fairness. The aim was to develop and internally validate sex-equitable machine learning (ML) models predicting 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, identify the most influential baseline prognostic markers, and audit sex-stratified model performance. One hundred physically active individuals (50 male, 50 female) with CAI (mean age 21.8 ± 2.3 years) were recruited from a university population between February 2017 and February 2018 and prospectively followed for 2 years; 96 (49 male, 47 female) with at least one follow-up response were retained for analysis (41 reinjury events, 43% reinjury rate). Fourteen baseline predictors spanning demographic, anthropometric, injury-history, patient-reported, biomechanical, postural-control, and functional-performance domains were collected. Six algorithms were trained with nested cross-validation: an unpenalized logistic regression baseline and five ML algorithms (Elastic Net, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Predictive contribution of each feature was quantified using Shapley additive explanations and partial-dependence plots. A pre-specified fairness audit compared single global and sex-specific Youden thresholds derived out-of-fold using the equalized-odds gap and disproportionate-impact ratio. All algorithms achieved area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.70; Elastic Net was selected as the primary model (AUC = 0.807, 95% CI 0.714-0.893; calibration slope = 1.015). Sex, arch height index, previous sprains, dorsiflexion range of motion, and Biodex Overall Stability Index consistently emerged as the most influential prognostic markers. Within-sex discrimination was comparable between males and females, but a single global threshold produced an equalized-odds gap of 0.384 that was reduced by 57% (to 0.164) through sex-specific thresholding without retraining the model. ML models with a fairness-audited threshold strategy predicted 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, reducing the equalized-odds gap by 57%, though the disproportionate-impact ratio (0.683) remained below the 0.80 benchmark. External validation is required before clinical deployment.

records.title: Short-term effects of resistive overground walking with a wearable hip exoskeleton on lower-limb strength and trunk muscle morphology in adults with high BMI: A pilot randomized trial.
records.abstract: BackgroundHigh body mass index (BMI) is associated with reduced physical function. The effects of resistive walking using wearable hip exoskeletons (WHEs) in overweight and obese individuals remain unclear.ObjectiveThis pilot randomized controlled trial evaluated the short-term effects of resistive overground walking with a wearable hip exoskeleton on lower-limb muscle strength and trunk muscle thickness in adults with a high BMI.MethodsTwenty-four participants with a high BMI were randomly assigned to the WHE or control group, with 22 participants completing the study (WHE, N = 12; control, N = 10). Both groups completed eight 60-min walking sessions over 2 weeks on a 2.4 km outdoor course. The WHE group used the resistance mode, whereas the control group used the inactive mode.ResultsImprovements in hip flexion, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion strength were greater in the WHE group (Cohen's d = 1.02-1.13), but these differences did not remain significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction. Transversus abdominis thickness did not differ between the groups. BMI reduction was greater in the WHE group, although this should be interpreted cautiously, given the short intervention duration.ConclusionResistive overground walking using WHEs numerically increased lower-limb strength in adults with high BMI, although no between-group differences remained significant after correction. Therefore, these findings should be regarded as exploratory.Clinical trial registration numberThis study was registered with the Korea Clinical Research Information Service (CRIS) under the registration number KCT0010895 (https://cris.nih.go.kr/cris/index/index.do).

records.title: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics identify distinct recovery phenotypes following ACL reconstruction: associations with function, pain, and psychological health.
records.abstract: Recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is typically monitored through patient-reported outcomes and periodic clinical assessments, which may not fully capture real-world functional performance. Smartphone-derived mobility data provide a passive and objective approach for evaluating daily activity and recovery. To examine associations between smartphone-derived mobility metrics and recovery outcomes in adults 3-12 months after primary ACL reconstruction and to identify distinct recovery phenotypes using mobility-based clustering. This cross-sectional study included 120 adults who were 3-12 months post-primary ACL reconstruction and had at least 14 days of retrospective smartphone mobility data. Mobility variables included daily step count, activity volume and intensity (e.g., active minutes and walking bout duration), sedentary behavior, and walking-related metrics. Outcomes included pain (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), functional status (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS] Pain, Activities of Daily Living, and Sport/Recreation subscales), knee-related quality of life (ACL Quality of Life questionnaire [ACL-QoL]), and psychological measures including the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Associations were evaluated using Pearson correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses. Recovery phenotypes were identified using unsupervised k-means clustering of mobility metrics. Higher daily step counts were independently associated with better KOOS-ADL scores (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), higher ACL-QoL scores (β = 0.45, p < 0.001), and lower pain intensity (β = - 0.39, p = 0.001). Three recovery phenotypes emerged: a high-activity/low-pain phenotype with superior function and minimal psychological distress, a moderate-activity/moderate-pain phenotype with intermediate outcomes, and a low-activity/high-pain phenotype characterized by reduced mobility, poorer function, greater pain, and higher pain catastrophizing. Significant gradients were observed across phenotypes for pain (NRS: 1.72-5.01), function (KOOS-Pain: 88.94-62.37), and pain catastrophizing (PCS: 8.52-24.91; all p < 0.001). Smartphone-derived mobility metrics were significantly associated with recovery outcomes following ACL reconstruction. Mobility-based clustering identified distinct recovery phenotypes associated with meaningful differences in pain, function, and pain catastrophizing, highlighting the potential of passive mobility monitoring to support personalized rehabilitation strategies. However, given the variability in evaluation periods and uncontrolled surgical factors, future research employing standardized, long-term follow-ups is warranted.

records.title: Superior canal dehiscence syndrome alters kinematics of head and postural control during standing.
records.abstract: Superior canal dehiscence syndrome (SCDS) is a peripheral vestibular disorder caused by a defect in the bony roof of the superior semicircular canal that alters inner-ear mechanics and produces abnormal vestibular stimulation and imbalance. Although postural instability is a prominent complaint in SCDS, how this disorder alters the kinematics of standing balance remains unclear. Here, we quantified how unilateral SCDS affects head and postural control during quiet standing using wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Angular velocities and linear accelerations were recorded from head and waist IMUs, enabling measurement of six-dimensional kinematics during seven standing balance tasks that systematically varied visual input and surface compliance. These measures revealed greater range and variability of head and waist motion in individuals with SCDS than in controls, indicating reduced stability during quiet standing. Group differences were greatest when visual and somatosensory feedback were degraded (e.g., standing on a foam surface with eyes closed), conditions that increase reliance on vestibular cues. Between-group differences were most consistently observed in pitch and roll kinematics, with increased yaw variability in several tasks. Variability in yaw head velocity correlated with oscillopsia and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, whereas variability of waist vertical acceleration and yaw velocity mainly correlated with greater contra-lesional amplitude of cervical vestibular myogenic potential and impaired gait function, respectively. Global kinematic scores derived from IMU data significantly differentiated individuals with SCDS from healthy controls. Together, these findings demonstrate that unilateral SCDS produces multiplanar balance impairments, and that wearable kinematic analysis may provide a sensitive approach for quantifying postural instability and identifying underlying mechanisms of balance difficulties, complementing current standard functional balance assessments. In addition, our findings have the potential to inform future balance rehabilitation and fall prevention research in individuals with SCDS. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-63082-1.

records.title: Syndesmotic screw fixation is associated with higher overall treatment costs when compared with suture button stabilisation in a single UK major trauma centre.
records.abstract: Ankle fractures frequently involve syndesmotic disruption, requiring stable fixation to restore joint function. Syndesmotic screw fixation remains widely used but carries significant drawbacks, including implant breakage, stiffness, and frequent need for removal. Suture button stabilisation offers clinical and economic advantages by preserving physiological motion and reducing reoperation rates. This study evaluates these costs under normal, unselected clinical practice, where implant choice and removal decisions were made independently by treating surgeons without protocol influence. This retrospective cohort study compares treatment costs of syndesmosis screw fixation and suture button stabilisation for syndesmotic injuries in a single UK Major Trauma Centre. 75 patients aged 16-60 years, with length stable or length stabilised ankle fractures with syndesmotic injuries, between October 2020 to October 2023 were included. The two cohorts were demographically similar and operative times were comparable (p = 0.170). Complications and reoperations were significantly higher with screw fixation (p < 0.001), with 56.8% undergoing removal, adding £31,460 in costs over three years. Overall, screw fixation cost £687 more per case than suture button stabilisation. Screw fixation became more costly when the hardware removal rate exceeded 8%. This dropped further to 2% when costs of additional follow up visits were also included. Despite a higher initial implant cost, suture button stabilisation demonstrated fewer complications and no hardware removals. In contrast, 56.8% of screw fixation cases underwent implant removal, leading to screw fixation costing £687 more per case on average, highlighting the superior clinical and economic value of suture button stabilisation in this pragmatic study.

records.title: Test-Retest Reliability of Soft Tissue Vibration Variables Across an Outdoor 5-km Run.
records.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the test-retest reliability of soft tissue vibration (STV) measurements taken superficial to the medial gastrocnemius during a 5-km outdoor run. Twenty-eight trained athlete participants (female: n = 14 and male: n = 14) wore a triaxial inertial measurement unit mounted on the skin superficial to their medial gastrocnemius (500 Hz) and performed two 5-km outdoor runs on different days at a controlled, individualized pace. STV outcome measures-peak acceleration, damping coefficient, settling time, peak and median frequency, and power-were analyzed using a continuous wavelet transform from averaged running strides within the entire run and among three 1500-m segments from each testing session. Intraclass correlation coefficients reinforced good to excellent between-day reliability measures (.75-.92) for all STV outcome measures except peak frequency (.50) and moderate to excellent reliability when comparing days across the 3 segments of the run (.70-.94), except for peak frequency (.44-.57). No significant day × time interactions were observed (P = .06-.63). Overall, STV outcome measures assessed with an inertial measurement unit during outdoor running demonstrated good reliability, supporting methodologies to quantify STV in real-world settings with potential applications in running performance and injury prevention research.

records.title: The impact of arthroscopic repair of the tibionavicular bundle of the deltoid ligament on ankle fractures.
records.abstract: Notwithstanding well-established ligament repair with ankle arthroscopy and a thorough understanding of deltoid ligament anatomy, evidence supporting early arthroscopic repair of the deltoid ligament (EAR-DL) remains limited. The purpose of this study was to compare EAR-DL with conservative treatment following ankle fracture. This retrospective study evaluated 45 patients with deltoid ligament tears among 1165 ankle fractures. Patients were grouped based on the EAR-DL decision or conservative treatment. The EAR-DL decision is based on evidence gathered from clinical, radiological, and surgical findings. Patients with imaging-confirmed deltoid ligament injury and ≥ 12 months of follow-up were included; those with major concomitant injuries were excluded. Clinical and radiological outcomes, including instability, functional scores, return to sport, and medial clear space (MCS), were compared. The concomitant injury count (CIC) was developed to measure injury complexity; yet this exploratory score has not yet been validated or assessed for reliability. Final outcomes were evaluated using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), controlling for baseline values. MCS ≤ 4 mm was considered normal, and ankle stability was assessed using anteromedial drawer and valgus stress tests. C3 was the most common fracture pattern in 14 patients (31.1%), followed by B3 in 9 patients (20.0%). The most common CIC level was 3, observed in 28 patients (62.2%). No recurrent instability occurred following EAR-DL, compared with 4 (15.4%) cases in the conservative group (p = 0.126). The return to sports was observed at an average of 33.04 ± 3.18 weeks in the conservative group and at 29.32 ± 1.60 weeks in the EAR-DL group (p < 0.001). In this retrospective cohort study, no statistically significant difference was found between the groups in recurrent instability. EAR-DL was associated with a smaller MCS and exploratory, unadjusted clinical outcomes compared with conservative management. Prospective, adequately powered studies are required to determine whether EAR-DL provides clinically meaningful benefits. Level III, retrospective cohort study.

records.title: The Impact of Hyperarch Fascia Training on Perceived Ankle Instability and Vertical Jump Performance in Physically Active Men and Women.
records.abstract: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) is a prevalent musculoskeletal condition that impairs physical performance and increases reinjury risk; yet, training programs emphasizing fascia-targeted techniques remain an understudied rehabilitation strategy. The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of 12 weeks of a multicomponent training intervention emphasizing fascia-targeted techniques (Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT)) on perceived ankle instability and function, and vertical jump performance in individuals with CAI. In this decentralized, randomized controlled trial, 66 participants were randomized (HFT n = 44, CON n = 22), with 43 participants completing the study and being analyzed (HFT n = 22; CON n = 21). Selected subjects confirmed perceived ankle instability (CAIT score ≤ 25) and were assigned to either a structured, multicomponent HFT program with various foot and ankle strengthening exercises, or a passive control condition instructed to maintain activities of daily living. The HFT group experienced disproportionately higher attrition (n = 22 excluded from analysis) than CON (n = 1 excluded from analysis due to becoming unresponsive). The reasons for attrition in the HFT group were due to becoming unresponsive (n = 13), self-reported difficulty with the protocol (n = 3), scheduling conflicts (n = 3), or adverse events (n = 3, reported as moderate). Outcomes were assessed at baseline, week 8, and week 12 using the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) (primary outcome), Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) (primary outcome), countermovement jump (CMJ) (secondary outcome), and Short Form Health Survey 12 (SF-12) (exploratory outcome). The HFT group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in CAIT scores compared to CON (group × time interaction p = 0.008), with large within-group effect sizes in the HFT group relative to baseline (d = 1.49 and 1.54, at weeks 8 and 12, respectively). Significant group × time interactions also favored HFT for CMJ jump height (p = 0.017) and flight time (p = 0.005) (co-secondary outcomes), as well as the CMJ algorithmic derivatives of mean velocity (p = 0.001) and take-off velocity (p = 0.008) (exploratory outcomes). No significant group × time interactions were observed for FAAM ADL or Sport subscales. Significant group × time interactions were found for SF-12 survey results for Physical Function (p = 0.045), Limits due to Physical Health (p = 0.030) and General Health (p = 0.043), with CON tending to decline over time and HFT tending to improve. The HFT group was higher than CON on Physical Function at Week 8 (d = 1.04, p = 0.009), and on Perceived Pain at Week 12 (d = 0.88, p = 0.047). Overall, these findings suggest that a multicomponent fascia-centered training program may represent a viable intervention for improving perceived ankle stability and increasing the explosive vertical jump performance in individuals with CAI.

records.title: The Relationship Between Kinesiophobia and Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Lateral Ankle Ligament Surgery.
records.abstract: Background/Objectives: Fear of reinjury and impaired psychological readiness frequently impede return to sport following lateral ankle ligament surgery. This study aimed to analyze the correlation between kinesiophobia and psychological readiness to return to sport before and after intensive rehabilitation in competitive athletes following lateral ankle ligament repair or reconstruction (LALRR). Methods: A prospective longitudinal pre-post observational study was conducted at a specialized sports rehabilitation center between January 2021 and January 2024. Forty-eight competitive athletes (Tegner score ≥ 7) who underwent LALRR completed a 3-week inpatient rehabilitation program (7 h daily). Kinesiophobia was evaluated using the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-17, TSK-13, TSK-11, and subscales), and psychological readiness was measured using the Ankle Ligament Reconstruction-Return to Sport after Injury (ALR-RSI) score at admission and discharge. Results: Cross-sectional analysis demonstrated weak to moderate negative correlations between ALR-RSI and TSK versions at baseline (rho = -0.28 to -0.43) and at discharge (rho = -0.20 to -0.60; TSK-13: rho = -0.60, 95% CI [-0.77, -0.34], p < 0.0001). Following rehabilitation, ALR-RSI scores significantly improved from 69.8 ± 17.3 to 76.1 ± 17.6 (p = 0.009), while TSK-17 scores decreased from 36.9 ± 7.8 to 33.2 ± 7.3 (p = 0.0001). However, the longitudinal correlation between individual change scores was weak and non-significant (rho = -0.15, 95% CI [-0.41, 0.11], p = 0.32). Conclusions: Kinesiophobia and psychological readiness exhibit weak to moderate inverse correlations cross-sectionally. However, no statistically significant association was detected between changes in kinesiophobia and psychological readiness in this sample (rho = -0.15, p = 0.32). These metrics capture distinct psychological aspects, and both should be monitored independently when assessing athletes prior to sports resumption.

records.title: Toward Wearable Joint Load Monitoring: Concurrent Estimation of Hip, Knee, and Ankle Sagittal Contact Forces from Sparse IMU Measurements.
records.abstract: Continuous monitoring of lower extremity joint contact forces is critical for rehabilitation medicine, sports injury prevention, and assistive device development. Yet, current wearable solutions often lack multi-joint integration or require cumbersome sensor arrays. This study aims to concurrently estimate hip, knee, and ankle sagittal compressive contact forces using a sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration across diverse daily activities. We collected data from 14 healthy adults equipped with four IMU sensors performing various daily movements, with reference contact forces captured using optical motion capture and force platforms. To estimate joint contact forces, we developed a domain-informed multi-task temporal convolutional network (Ada-Att-MTCN). This architecture integrates a shared temporal convolutional network encoder, task-specific attention mechanisms, homoscedastic uncertainty-based dynamic task weighting, and a soft physiological-bound penalty. Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-subject-out nested cross-validation against 4 baseline methods, with root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) as evaluation metrics. On the self-collected dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN achieved the highest accuracy across all activities, with mean RMSEs of 0.328 ± 0.13 BW (hip), 0.380 ± 0.09 BW (knee), and 0.365 ± 0.15 BW (ankle), and an average R2 of 0.822 ± 0.10. On the external dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN likewise performed best among all methods (average R² = 0.754 ± 0.05). The proposed framework captures complex inter-joint dynamics, enabling robust simultaneous load estimation with drastically reduced hardware complexity. This approach provides a practical, non-invasive solution for transitioning lab-grade multi-joint load monitoring to wearable deployment in rehabilitation and sports medicine.

records.title: Tracking Recovery After TKA with Instrumented Timed Up and Go: Spatiotemporal, Rotational, and Strength Adaptations over Six Months.
records.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) improves pain and functional mobility, although gait impairments may persist postoperatively. This study investigated longitudinal changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and gait performance using an instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) test with wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Twenty-two patients with end-stage KOA were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score five-subscale composite (KOOS5) showed a significant overall change over time (p < 0.001), while isometric muscle strength showed significant overall changes across all tested muscle groups (p ≤ 0.008), with mean values demonstrating an initial postoperative decline followed by subsequent increases. Total TUG duration showed a significant overall time effect (p = 0.023), with significant reductions observed in the forward and return gait phases (p = 0.012 and p = 0.001, respectively). End-turning maximum rotational speed and sit-to-stand vertical acceleration showed significant overall time effects (p = 0.012 and p = 0.024, respectively), whereas the remaining parameters did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that recovery following TKA is multidimensional, with significant changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and functional mobility. iTUG analysis identified phase-specific changes, while several turning and transitional parameters did not show significant longitudinal changes, supporting the use of targeted rehabilitation strategies focusing on dynamic stability and movement control.

records.title: Using Wearable Sensors and Video Analysis to Improve Functional Electrical Stimulation Prescription in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Series.
records.abstract: A growing body of evidence supports the use of functional electrical stimulation (FES) in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). However, prescription remains an imprecise process with no well-established guidelines for assessing the immediate or long-term effects to ensure maximum benefit. The purpose of this case series was to assess the potential benefits of using wearable sensors and video analysis to provide immediate feedback on gait performance to improve FES prescription in people with MS. Three adults (2 women, 1 man; age range, 39-62 years) with MS with varying levels of lower extremity motor function and gait impairment were enrolled. During a single visit, participants performed a series of 10-m walks under various FES and non-FES conditions while using wearable motion sensors. Additionally, 2D video analysis was used to assess alterations in knee angles during swing and stance phases. All participants demonstrated improvements in a variety of gait variables, including a clinically meaningful (> 0.1 m/s) increase in gait speed during 1 or more of the FES conditions when compared with the no-device and/or prescribed ankle foot orthosis conditions. There were additional improvements associated with multichannel stimulation of the lower leg and thigh for certain gait variables. Data from the wearable sensors and video analysis were advantageous in helping researchers determine the most appropriate FES prescription for each participant. This case series demonstrates the potential clinical usefulness of these technologies in prescribing FES for people with MS.

records.title: Wearable sensing technologies and machine learning for fatigue assessment in sport horses.
records.abstract: Fatigue in sport horses is a multifactorial phenomenon that critically affects performance, injury risk, and welfare, yet its real-time, field-based assessment remains an unmet challenge. To synthesise evidence on the use of wearable sensors and machine learning for fatigue-related monitoring in sport horses and to identify priorities for future fatigue assessment. Scoping review. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Publications from 2015 to 2026 were identified through Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. Evidence from 102 publications was synthesised across five sensing modalities-heart rate (HR)/heart rate variability (HRV), thermometry, inertial measurement units (IMUs), surface electromyography (sEMG), and GPS-alongside machine learning applications for feature extraction, state classification, and risk modelling. Our synthesis reveals a fundamental disconnect: while each technology captures distinct physiological or biomechanical correlates of load, including autonomic response, thermoregulatory strain, gait stability, neuromuscular activation, and external workload, none provides a standalone signature of fatigue. Only a minority of studies used fatigue as a direct modelling label, with most relying on proxy outcomes such as asymmetry or performance decrement. The included literature was heterogeneous in sensor modalities, study designs, outcome measures, and application contexts. In addition, the limited use of directly defined fatigue outcomes restricted comparison across studies and constrained conclusions regarding fatigue-specific monitoring. The path forward lies not in developing yet another single-sensor solution, but in establishing a multidimensional, context-aware framework that integrates complementary data streams, individualised baselines, and interpretable models. Future research should prioritise: (1) operationalised fatigue definitions; (2) longitudinal, within-horse monitoring designs; (3) robust multimodal fusion architectures; (4) rigorous external validation across equestrian disciplines; and (5) explainable artificial intelligence to bridge the gap between algorithmic output and actionable training decisions.

records.title: Weightbearing CT in the Evaluation of Athletic Foot and Ankle Injuries.
records.abstract: Subtle foot and ankle injuries in athletes, including syndesmotic sprains, ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, may be underestimated or misclassified on conventional imaging. This review summarizes the current role of weightbearing CT (WBCT) in their evaluation, focusing on quantitative parameters, recent technical advances, and their potential influence on clinical decision-making. Recent evidence has shifted WBCT from qualitative assessment toward reproducible three-dimensional quantification. Volumetric assessment and distance mapping improve characterization of syndesmotic instability, while external-rotation stress can reveal abnormalities not evident during neutral standing. In the midfoot, triplanar realignment and side-to-side comparison improve the reliability of Lisfranc measurements and support detection of subtle instability. Distance mapping permits reproducible quantification of osteochondral lesion surface area, depth, and volume and may improve consistency in surgical planning. WBCT has also characterized sport-specific alignment patterns and a morphologic and bone-density phenotype associated with proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures. Semiautomated segmentation and deep-learning methods may further reduce observer dependence and analysis time. WBCT provides three-dimensional measurements under physiologic load that complement clinical examination and conventional imaging in selected athletic foot and ankle conditions. Its greatest current value lies in characterizing subtle instability, malalignment, and osseous morphology when these findings may alter treatment planning. However, most available evidence is retrospective and derived from symptomatic or injured cohorts. Prospective studies are needed to validate diagnostic thresholds, determine whether WBCT-derived parameters predict injury or outcomes, and define their role in routine athletic screening and return-to-sport decision-making.
